cards.title: Media Matching: Modern Social Algorithms Are Matchmaking Engines, Not Follow Networks
cards.summary: Since 2020 (TikTok-driven), platform algorithms only match video topics with viewers' historical interests, regardless of who follows you, so store content strategy must shift from 'publish to my followers' to 'help the algorithm find the right strangers'.
cards.use_when: When deciding the content direction for a store account on Instagram/TikTok/YouTube, or diagnosing why follower count is decent but organic traffic and conversion are not improving.
steps: Think of the algorithm as a business that makes money from ad watch time: Instagram/YouTube/TikTok only earn ad revenue when viewers keep watching, so their sole goal is to push videos viewers like and prolong sessions.

Your job is therefore not 'gaining followers' but helping the algorithm match your video to the specific audience most likely to finish and engage—the more accurate the match, the more distribution the algorithm gives you.

Under this framework, follower count no longer determines exposure; a video can be pushed to strangers who don't know you at all. So don't limit your topic ambition because of a small follower base, and don't assume content will be distributed just because you have many followers.

Treat each video as a 'topic-audience' pairing declaration: use spoken content and captions to clearly state what topic you're covering and for whom, because the algorithm mainly judges topics based on video transcription and captions.

Review your account's last 20 videos: do the topics point to the same audience avatar? If topics are scattered, fix topic focus first; if topics are already consistent but data is still poor, then the problem falls on content quality (script, editing, topic value).

Apply this principle to store operations: if your product is camping gear, consistently produce specific topics like 'camping gear selection/wild cooking' rather than camping today and office outfits tomorrow.
caveats: This is a creator's empirical interpretation of platform algorithms, not official documentation; platform mechanisms change, and specific recommendation rules should be based on current public platform information.

The author claims to have achieved millions of followers/billions of views across platforms, which is a personal track record statement and does not mean following the method will necessarily produce the same results.

cards.title: Militant Topic Discipline: Train the Algorithm with 30–50 Videos on the Same Topic
cards.summary: Post 30–50 videos on the same topic and same audience avatar consecutively on the same account, so the algorithm's transcription and caption analysis can steadily build a lookalike audience.
cards.use_when: When planning a content calendar for a store account, or determining the topic scope for the first ten weeks before cold-starting a new account.
steps: One account, one topic area only. If you like sports, tech, and design simultaneously, don't rotate posts among these three topics—the algorithm won't know who to push you to.
Lock in a specific customer avatar for that topic, and start topic selection from that avatar's pain points rather than speaking broadly about industry trends.

Use 'precision' as the only standard: both spoken content and captions must clearly tell the algorithm 'what topic I'm discussing and to whom,' because the algorithm judges topics from transcription and captions, then pushes videos to lookalikes of highly engaged audiences.

Commit to a sufficiently long continuous period: after 30–50 consecutive same-topic videos using this method, the algorithm will learn your topic and push you into the corresponding community; this is the source's empirical threshold, not a platform-published number.

Clarify three prohibitions: do not mix multiple topics on one account; do not make content that is valueless or uninteresting to the target avatar; do not make generalized content unrelated to that avatar.

For ecommerce application: treat the 'account' as an entry point for a product category or solution, not a universal brand mouthpiece. If selling pet supplies, focus long-term on one sub-segment (e.g., cat staple food), not cats, dogs, birds, and fish all together.
caveats: 30–50 videos is the author's empirical heuristic threshold; the platform has not published this number, so don't treat it as a guaranteed value.
Topic focus solves the problem of 'being pushed to the right people,' not content quality, scripts, or retention; when data is still poor after accurate targeting, turn to the content itself.
When a brand has multiple categories, it needs separate accounts or content lines for different topics; don't cram them into one account.

cards.title: On-Target Virality: Maximize Penetration Within a Niche Slice, Not Broad-Spectrum Hits
cards.summary: For business growth, pursue high penetration only within the target avatar slice, not 10M views across audiences, because broad-spectrum hits confuse the algorithm's judgment of 'who to push to.'
cards.use_when: When evaluating whether a store content topic is worth doing, or reviewing high-view videos that brought no sales.
steps: Distinguish two types of virality: pure virality chooses extremely broad, universally relatable topics to expand the audience pool at all costs (most 10M+ views come from here); on-target virality maximizes penetration within a very narrow audience slice without spilling outside that slice.
Use the '800-million-person pie' metaphor for trade-offs: pure virality wants people outside the slice to watch; on-target virality only wants to cover as many people inside the slice as possible.

When selecting topics, ask of every idea: will my core audience avatar find this interesting, useful, valuable, or entertaining? If the answer is no, don't post it even if it might go viral—the multiple audience groups brought by broad-spectrum hits will confuse the algorithm's direction for your next video.

Remember the algorithm prefers precision over breadth: it would rather let a 'fan favorite' in a niche category receive continuous distribution than be broadly pushed to all consumers of broadly related content.

Trade deep trust for conversion: narrowly and specifically addressing users' concrete pain points builds trust and drives purchases more easily than broad generalization; the source observed small creators (hundreds of thousands of followers) building seven-figure businesses through niche cult fandom, while some 7-million-follower accounts struggle to make a living—this is a case comparison, not a promise.
In execution, pair a narrow topic with a category-related broad case shell to expand penetration within the slice, but the core pain point must target the avatar.
caveats: The author explicitly says they still want virality, just aimed at their own category; this is not an absolute rule of 'rejecting hits.'
The seven-figure business and 'big accounts can't pay rent' are comparative cases and do not constitute causal guarantees.

If the brand's goal is broad exposure, recruitment, or volume scaling (e.g., creative testing for ads), the criteria for broad content may differ from direct ecommerce conversion, and trade-offs should be made by goal.

cards.title: Fish Where the Fish Are: Focus on One Hero Platform Plus Email for Six Months
cards.summary: Don't spread across all platforms at first: choose one platform with the highest customer density plus email, go deep for six consecutive months, and confirm where the fish are through customer research.
cards.use_when: When a new store or new account decides which social platform to invest limited time and budget in.
steps: Reject generalized advice like 'you must be on every platform because you don't know where buyers are.' The author believes buyers are on one of six platforms: Facebook, YouTube, LinkedIn, TikTok, Instagram, X.
Find the one platform with the highest customer density as your hero platform and add email (email is the only other leg recommended alongside it); operate only this combination for six months.

Concentrate all attention on one platform to immerse yourself in that platform's community and zeitgeist: comment on others' posts in the same field on that platform, reply to all your own comments, and use the platform's secondary formats (e.g., use Stories when mainly doing Reels).
On the chosen platform, use video as the primary format (short or long video both work) and stay as consistent as possible with updates.

If unsure where customers are: randomly sample a small portion of existing customers and ask directly which platform they are most active on; or conversely, think about whom you follow and where you learn the most about your industry.

For ecommerce implications: rather than posting perfunctorily on six platforms, establish a 'regular' status in the category on one platform, then layer email to turn attention into a repeatable owned asset.
caveats: 'Six platforms' and 'six months' are the author's empirical claims, not platform data or industry benchmarks.
If a store already has a mature team and multi-platform resources, the logic of single-platform focus may not apply.
Without a core team, multiple platforms simultaneously increase execution complexity—this is the author's observation from working with hundreds of business owners.

cards.title: Islands vs. Ecosystems: Treat Platforms as Islands and Don't Cross-Promote
cards.summary: Social platforms are independent, punish external links, and users don't want to switch apps, so content should be native on each island; the only bridge to build is from rented social land to owned assets (email/private domain).
cards.use_when: When deciding whether to post a YouTube link in Reels or paste X/TikTok content in Stories, and when designing a social-to-private-domain funnel.
steps: Treat each platform as an independent island, not an interconnected ecosystem. Platform owners compete with each other (Meta's Instagram doesn't want to send users to Google's YouTube), so they reward behavior that keeps users on-site.

Expect external link penalties: placing a URL in a tweet or LinkedIn post will 'cut' engagement, and placing a URL in Stories does the same; platforms do this because they don't make money once users leave. Regarding creators' claims that 'sacrificing single-post reach for all-platform growth is worth it,' the author explicitly disagrees.

Consider differences in user consumption habits: each platform is like a car at a different speed (the author gives examples: Instagram like 35mph, TikTok like 50mph, YouTube like 10mph); users go to a platform precisely because they like its consumption experience and algorithmic community; forcing people elsewhere often makes them hit it and churn, or even stop watching your content altogether.
The only 'ramp' to build is from rented to owned: Instagram to email, Instagram to private community is fine; island-to-island like Instagram to TikTok is not.

If you still want a unified brand across platforms, use 'world building' rather than forcing: keep visuals and narrative consistent so users feel it lines up when they discover you natively, but don't force them to migrate.

For ecommerce execution: prioritize social traffic to PDP toward email subscription, private community, or your own site, rather than 'transferring' Instagram viewers to another social account of yours.
caveats: External links being 'completely throttled' is the author's empirical description; each platform's handling of external links and URL placement restrictions changes, so verify by testing on current platforms.
This advice targets individuals/small teams starting from zero; established cross-platform brands may operate differently.
The 'speed' metaphor only illustrates differences in consumption pace, not measured data.

cards.title: Media Layer Monetization Trap: Attention Is at the Media Layer, Value Is at the Platform and Supply Layers
cards.summary: The content stack has platform, media, and supply layers; value is mainly captured by the platform and supply layers. Creators relying only on AdSense and sponsorships have limited income; media should be treated as an attention engine directed to owned products/services.
cards.use_when: When planning monetization for a store account, or evaluating whether content production is worth treating as a primary income source.
steps: Understand the three-layer content stack: the bottom is the platform layer (Instagram, TikTok, YouTube), the middle is the media layer (creators producing content), and the top is the supply layer (brands making products/services and paying creators for traffic).
Recognize that attention is generated by the media layer, but value is rarely captured there—all attention comes from the media layer, yet money mainly lands in the platform and supply layers.

The reason is that value capture correlates with risk: starting media is easier than building a brand, and building a successful social platform is extremely hard, so creator payout rates are low and captured value is low. The author uses personal experience: 12 months and hundreds of hours yielded about $52 from YouTube AdSense, then occasional $500–1000 brand deals; views and followers were high but income did not match expectations.

Treat media as a means to acquire attention, not the endpoint: direct attention to owned products, services, or affiliate partnerships with no income ceiling, rather than relying on capped or restricted income like AdSense CPM or brand deals.

For ecommerce practice: store account content KPIs should prioritize clicks and conversions to owned products, not just views or platform revenue shares; treat content as a free acquisition channel for owned products.
caveats: The $52, $500–1000, etc. are the author's personal experience figures, a case rather than a universal benchmark.

This is not saying brand deals are worthless, but that they shouldn't be treated as a primary income source; for stores specifically, also calculate based on owned product margins and content production costs.
